questions.question: Which statement about Independent-groups gain test is INACCURATE?
options: A within-person calculation does not make independent groups paired with each other.
A justified comparison of gain values from distinct participant groups.
Gains from different participants always require a paired test merely because each gain uses two scores.
An illustration is: Two therapy groups' gains are compared under appropriate assumptions.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: Gains from different participants always require a paired test merely because each gain uses two scores.
A justified comparison of gain values from distinct participant groups.
Example: Two therapy groups' gains are compared under appropriate assumptions.
Important distinction: A within-person calculation does not make independent groups paired with each other.

questions.question: Which statement about Paired analysis is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: A within-group pre-post difference is analyzed using paired observations.
A paired within-group result by itself establishes superiority over another group.
Within-group change and between-group treatment difference answer different questions.
Analysis accounting for linked observations within the same participant or matched pair.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: A paired within-group result by itself establishes superiority over another group.
Analysis accounting for linked observations within the same participant or matched pair.
Example: A within-group pre-post difference is analyzed using paired observations.
Important distinction: Within-group change and between-group treatment difference answer different questions.
questions.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

questions.question: Which statement about Welch t test is INACCURATE?
options: Select the test variant according to design and assumptions.
Every t test requires a pooled equal-variance assumption.
A two-mean comparison that does not impose equal group variances.
An illustration is: Independent gain distributions with unequal variances are compared appropriately.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: Every t test requires a pooled equal-variance assumption.
A two-mean comparison that does not impose equal group variances.
Example: Independent gain distributions with unequal variances are compared appropriately.
Important distinction: Select the test variant according to design and assumptions.

questions.question: Which statement about One-way ANOVA is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: A single factor defines three treatment groups.
A significant omnibus result identifies every pairwise difference without further analysis.
An omnibus comparison and specific contrasts require distinct interpretation.
A model comparing group means for one factor under stated assumptions.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: A significant omnibus result identifies every pairwise difference without further analysis.
A model comparing group means for one factor under stated assumptions.
Example: A single factor defines three treatment groups.
Important distinction: An omnibus comparison and specific contrasts require distinct interpretation.

questions.question: Which statement about Baseline-adjusted analysis is INACCURATE?
options: Baseline adjustment is forbidden in all nonrandomized studies and automatically unbiased in all randomized studies.
Modelling follow-up outcomes while accounting for baseline and other justified covariates.
An illustration is: An ANCOVA estimates a conditional group contrast.
Specify the estimand and assumptions; neither blanket rejection nor automatic causal confidence is justified.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: Baseline adjustment is forbidden in all nonrandomized studies and automatically unbiased in all randomized studies.
Modelling follow-up outcomes while accounting for baseline and other justified covariates.
Example: An ANCOVA estimates a conditional group contrast.
Important distinction: Specify the estimand and assumptions; neither blanket rejection nor automatic causal confidence is justified.

questions.question: Which statement about Normality and sample size is INACCURATE?
options: Every raw data set becomes normally distributed once n reaches thirty.
Large-sample approximations have conditions and do not transform the observations.
An illustration is: A large sample of skewed observations remains skewed as raw data.
A distinction between an observation distribution and sampling-distribution approximations.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: Every raw data set becomes normally distributed once n reaches thirty.
A distinction between an observation distribution and sampling-distribution approximations.
Example: A large sample of skewed observations remains skewed as raw data.
Important distinction: Large-sample approximations have conditions and do not transform the observations.
questions.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

questions.question: Which statement about Cohen standardized mean difference is INACCURATE?
options: State the denominator convention and examine uncertainty and functional relevance.
An illustration is: A two-point mean difference divided by SD four equals 0.5.
A difference in means expressed relative to a stated standard deviation convention.
A standardized effect size itself proves meaningful improvement for every client.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: A standardized effect size itself proves meaningful improvement for every client.
A difference in means expressed relative to a stated standard deviation convention.
Example: A two-point mean difference divided by SD four equals 0.5.
Important distinction: State the denominator convention and examine uncertainty and functional relevance.

questions.question: Which statement about Hedges g is INACCURATE?
options: An illustration is: A correction factor adjusts an appropriate standardized mean difference.
The small-sample correction is central; denominator choices must also be specified.
Hedges g differs from Cohen d solely because it uses any pooled standard deviation.
A standardized mean-difference estimator with a small-sample bias correction.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: Hedges g differs from Cohen d solely because it uses any pooled standard deviation.
A standardized mean-difference estimator with a small-sample bias correction.
Example: A correction factor adjusts an appropriate standardized mean difference.
Important distinction: The small-sample correction is central; denominator choices must also be specified.
questions.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

questions.question: Which statement about Individual change versus group average is INACCURATE?
options: A positive group mean proves every participant improved equally.
An illustration is: The same mean gain can combine diverse individual outcomes.
Inspect distributions and individual patterns instead of relying only on averages.
The distinction between participant-level change and a group summary.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: A positive group mean proves every participant improved equally.
The distinction between participant-level change and a group summary.
Example: The same mean gain can combine diverse individual outcomes.
Important distinction: Inspect distributions and individual patterns instead of relying only on averages.

questions.question: Which statement about Functional participation outcome is INACCURATE?
options: Measurement of meaningful involvement in everyday communication activities.
Different outcome domains can complement one another without being interchangeable.
An illustration is: A caregiver report complements a targeted grammar probe.
Change on an impairment probe automatically captures every everyday participation benefit.
questions.explanation:
The inaccurate claim is: Change on an impairment probe automatically captures every everyday participation benefit.
Measurement of meaningful involvement in everyday communication activities.
Example: A caregiver report complements a targeted grammar probe.
Important distinction: Different outcome domains can complement one another without being interchangeable.

questions.question: Which statement about Sensitivity analysis is INACCURATE?
options: Report prespecified or justified alternatives rather than fishing for favourable findings.
An illustration is: Alternative justified approaches are compared transparently.
Sensitivity analysis means retaining only the model that produces a significant result.
Examination of how conclusions change under plausible analytical choices or assumptions.

The inaccurate claim is: Sensitivity analysis means retaining only the model that produces a significant result.
Examination of how conclusions change under plausible analytical choices or assumptions.
Example: Alternative justified approaches are compared transparently.
Important distinction: Report prespecified or justified alternatives rather than fishing for favourable findings.

options: A distinction between teaching examples and observations from real participants.

The inaccurate claim is: A tutorial's invented teaching dataset proves that its hypothetical treatment works clinically.

questions.question: Two independent participant groups each supply individual pre-post gains. What determines whether their gain comparison is paired?
options: Whether observations are linked between groups, not merely whether each gain uses two scores.
The presence of any pretest makes groups paired automatically.
The use of subtraction guarantees matching across participants.
questions.explanation: Each person's gain contains repeated measures, but different participants' gains can form independent groups. Choose analysis for the comparison's actual dependency structure.

questions.question: A small p value and a large standardized effect are reported from artificial tutorial data. What can be concluded about real efficacy?
options: The artificial sample represents every child in Lahore.
The calculations illustrate analysis but do not establish real treatment effectiveness.
No effect-size assumption matters for invented data.
The hypothetical treatment has been clinically proven.
questions.explanation: The supplied PDF explicitly uses a hypothetical scenario and artificial scores. Distinguish teaching computations from observations supporting clinical conclusions.

questions.question: Which statement corrects the idea that n = 30 makes data normal?
options: Larger samples can support some approximations but do not transform raw observations into a normal distribution.
All statistical assumptions vanish at n = 30.
Every 30 observations must follow a perfect normal curve.
Thirty observations guarantee sufficient power for every effect.
questions.explanation: The central-limit idea concerns sampling distributions under conditions, not automatic normality of observations. Examine design, distributions and relevant model assumptions.

concepts.definition: Planned inquiry using explicit procedures to answer a question through evidence.
concepts.example: A clinician specifies recruitment, measurement and analysis before collecting treatment data.
concepts.false: Research is any opinion expressed confidently by an experienced person.
concepts.note: A defensible conclusion follows a transparent method rather than confidence or anecdote alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Integration of research evidence, clinical expertise and client or caregiver perspectives.
concepts.example: An SLP combines trial findings with clinical judgment and family priorities.
concepts.false: Evidence-based practice requires ignoring the client's values whenever a trial exists.
concepts.note: Evidence informs decisions together with expertise, circumstances and the client's priorities.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Professional judgment developed through training, practice and critical reflection.
concepts.example: A clinician judges whether a study's procedure fits a particular client's situation.
concepts.false: Clinical expertise makes appraisal of research permanently unnecessary.
concepts.note: Expertise helps interpret and apply evidence rather than replace all external checking.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Information collected about the individual client's performance or response.
concepts.example: Repeated communication probes show how one client responds during therapy.
concepts.false: Internal evidence means only unpublished rumours about a hospital.
concepts.note: Systematic client observations complement external research and require sound measurement.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Findings obtained from investigations beyond the individual clinical encounter.
concepts.example: A clinician consults published comparative studies before selecting an approach.
concepts.false: Every published finding is automatically applicable to every client.
concepts.note: Appraisal and population fit determine how useful external findings are locally.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An issue or uncertainty that motivates systematic investigation.
concepts.example: Limited knowledge about rural access to SLP services motivates a study.
concepts.false: A research problem is the same thing as the final statistical result.
concepts.note: The problem motivates the question; results arise only after investigation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A statement of what a study intends to accomplish.
concepts.example: The study aims to compare vocabulary change between two delivery formats.
concepts.false: An objective guarantees that its expected finding will occur.
concepts.note: An aim guides inquiry without predetermining what the evidence must show.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A written plan for design, participants, procedures, outcomes and analysis.
concepts.example: The team documents how children will be recruited and assessed.
concepts.false: A protocol is merely the reference list added after publication.
concepts.note: Planning supports accountability and makes deviations visible when they occur.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Practical achievability given time, participants, resources, skills and constraints.
concepts.example: A student checks whether enough eligible participants can be recruited this semester.
concepts.false: A scientifically interesting question is automatically feasible in every clinic.
concepts.note: Importance must be balanced against recruitment, resources and ethical constraints.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A planning mnemonic emphasizing specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound goals.
concepts.example: A project defines one outcome and a realistic collection deadline.
concepts.false: Every qualitative question must be reduced to a numerical endpoint to be legitimate.
concepts.note: SMART can support planning without replacing the logic of qualitative inquiry.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A schedule allocating time to linked stages of a project.
concepts.example: Ethics review is scheduled before recruitment and data collection.
concepts.false: Recruitment should begin before ethical requirements are considered.
concepts.note: Dependencies and realistic approval time belong in the research schedule.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A voluntary decision based on understandable information about participation.
concepts.example: An adult receives accessible information and can decline without losing usual care.
concepts.false: A signature alone proves comprehension and freedom from pressure.
concepts.note: Consent is an ongoing communication process, not just a signed form.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Protecting identifiable participant information against unauthorized disclosure.
concepts.example: Recordings are stored with restricted access and coded identifiers.
concepts.false: Coding a recording makes recognition of the speaker impossible in all circumstances.
concepts.note: Voice and contextual details can remain identifying despite removal of a name.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Control over access to a person and their personal circumstances.
concepts.example: Interviews are conducted where others cannot overhear sensitive accounts.
concepts.false: Privacy concerns only whether the final bibliography is alphabetized.
concepts.note: Protecting the encounter and protecting stored information are related but distinct.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A condition where identity is not known or cannot reasonably be linked to responses.
concepts.example: An unlinked survey collects no identifiers or recognizable contextual details.
concepts.false: All confidential interview studies are necessarily anonymous to the interviewer.
concepts.note: An interviewer can know identities while still maintaining confidentiality.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An ethical commitment to promote benefits and minimize avoidable harm.
concepts.example: Researchers reduce unnecessary burden while evaluating potential scientific value.
concepts.false: Beneficence requires promising direct improvement to every participant.
concepts.note: Potential benefit does not justify misleading promises or disproportionate risk.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Fair distribution of research burdens and benefits and equitable selection.
concepts.example: Recruitment criteria are justified rather than excluding a group merely for convenience.
concepts.false: Justice means enrolling only the easiest-to-reach clients in every study.
concepts.note: Fair inclusion requires scientific and ethical justification, not identical treatment regardless of needs.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Independent assessment of a study's ethical acceptability before relevant activities begin.
concepts.example: A research committee reviews the protocol before recruitment.
concepts.false: Approval removes the team's responsibility to monitor participant welfare.
concepts.note: Ethical duties continue after review, and important changes may require further review.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Adapting consent communication and seeking developmentally appropriate agreement where applicable.
concepts.example: A team uses supported communication and appropriate child assent procedures.
concepts.false: A communication impairment automatically proves inability to decide about research.
concepts.note: Capacity must be assessed appropriately; language difficulty alone does not establish incapacity.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The proportion of a defined population with a condition at a specified time or period.
concepts.example: A school survey estimates how many pupils currently meet stated criteria.
concepts.false: Prevalence counts only newly occurring cases during follow-up.
concepts.note: Existing cases define prevalence; new occurrence defines incidence.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: New occurrence of a condition among people at risk over a specified period.
concepts.example: Researchers follow initially unaffected pupils to identify newly arising cases.
concepts.false: Incidence and prevalence always have the same numerator.
concepts.note: Define the at-risk population and time interval or person-time explicitly.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Structured evaluation of a study's validity, relevance and interpretation.
concepts.example: A reader checks allocation, measures, missing data and applicability.
concepts.false: Peer review guarantees that critical appraisal is no longer needed.
concepts.note: Publication does not remove the need to evaluate methods and limitations.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The sum of numerical values divided by their number.
concepts.example: Scores 2, 4 and 9 have a mean of 5.
concepts.false: The mean is necessarily equal to the most frequent observation.
concepts.note: Outliers can pull the mean away from the middle of the ordered data.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The middle ordered value, or the average of two middle values for an even count.
concepts.example: The median of 1, 2 and 12 is 2.
concepts.false: The median must change greatly whenever one extreme observation increases.
concepts.note: The median is often less sensitive to extreme values than the mean.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The most frequently occurring value or category.
concepts.example: Diagnosis B occurs more often than any other category.
concepts.false: The mode can only be calculated for ratio-scale measurements.
concepts.note: Frequencies can identify a mode for nominal categories too.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The spread of observations rather than their central location.
concepts.example: Two groups have the same mean but very different score ranges.
concepts.false: Equal means guarantee that every participant has a similar score.
concepts.note: Range, variance and standard deviation describe different aspects of spread.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A decision relative to a prespecified threshold for a test under its model.
concepts.example: A prespecified two-sided test returns p below the selected alpha.
concepts.false: A small p value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
concepts.note: A p value concerns data at least as extreme under the null model and assumptions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An interval produced by a procedure with stated long-run coverage under assumptions.
concepts.example: A 95% procedure covers a fixed population parameter in 95% of repeated samples.
concepts.false: A computed frequentist 95% interval assigns a 95% probability to its fixed parameter.
concepts.note: Interpret coverage through the procedure; also consider the interval's width and assumptions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The practical value of a change for functioning, participation or client priorities.
concepts.example: A family reports that gains improve everyday classroom communication.
concepts.false: Any statistically significant difference must be clinically meaningful.
concepts.note: Consider magnitude, uncertainty, everyday impact and client judgment together.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Sharing findings through appropriate reports, presentations or other channels.
concepts.example: Researchers report a null finding with its limitations.
concepts.false: Only positive results should be shared with the research community.
concepts.note: Transparent dissemination reduces selective visibility of favourable findings.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Organization of a report into introduction, methods, results and discussion.
concepts.example: A paper separates procedures from findings and interpretation.
concepts.false: The discussion is the appropriate place to hide unreported data-collection methods.
concepts.note: Clear sections help readers distinguish what was planned, observed and inferred.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Evaluation of a manuscript by relevant experts to inform editorial decisions.
concepts.example: Reviewers identify weaknesses and request justified revisions.
concepts.false: Acceptance certifies that every published conclusion is permanently correct.
concepts.note: Peer review can improve a report but does not eliminate errors or uncertainty.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A request for support justified by a research plan, resources and intended contribution.
concepts.example: A budget explains the need for assessment and participant-travel costs.
concepts.false: A persuasive proposal can replace a feasible research method.
concepts.note: Fundability depends on scientific value, feasibility and a justified use of resources.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Coordination of complementary expertise and responsibilities in a project.
concepts.example: An SLP and statistician plan outcome analysis together.
concepts.false: Collaboration permits leaving authorship and data responsibilities undefined.
concepts.note: Agree roles, communication, data access and appropriate credit in advance.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Systematic measurement of progress against defined goals.
concepts.example: A clinician repeats a specified functional communication measure.
concepts.false: Improvement observed once proves that the intervention caused it.
concepts.note: Repeated monitoring documents change, while causal attribution needs suitable design.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec# 01. Introduction to research.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A broad orientation such as quantitative, qualitative or mixed methods.
concepts.example: A project combines numerical comparison with interpretation of caregiver accounts.
concepts.false: A questionnaire is automatically the entire philosophical approach of a study.
concepts.note: Approach, design and specific procedures operate at distinguishable levels.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The organized strategy connecting a question to evidence and inference.
concepts.example: A randomized comparison specifies how treatment groups will be formed and measured.
concepts.false: Design means only choosing a font for the results table.
concepts.note: Design structures the inquiry rather than merely its presentation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A specific procedure for collecting, analyzing or interpreting evidence.
concepts.example: A researcher uses semi-structured interviews and an explicit coding process.
concepts.false: Using interviews always determines one unique methodology.
concepts.note: The same procedure can serve different designs when used for different purposes.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Inquiry using numerical measurement to describe patterns or test relationships.
concepts.example: Researchers compare mean intelligibility scores between defined groups.
concepts.false: Every quantitative study necessarily manipulates a treatment.
concepts.note: Numerical studies can be observational, descriptive or experimental.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Inquiry interpreting meanings, experiences and processes within context.
concepts.example: Interviews explore how adults experience workplace communication barriers.
concepts.false: Qualitative research has no systematic procedures or need for evidence.
concepts.note: Rigorous qualitative work makes sampling, analysis and interpretation transparent.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Intentional integration of quantitative and qualitative components.
concepts.example: Interviews help explain unexpected differences found in a survey.
concepts.false: Merely adding an unrelated quotation to a statistical report ensures integration.
concepts.note: State how components connect and what combined inference they support.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Reasoning from observations toward patterns or more general accounts.
concepts.example: Repeated interview patterns inform the development of explanatory themes.
concepts.false: Induction begins by proving a fixed hypothesis without examining observations.
concepts.note: Inductive interpretations remain open to contrary cases and refinement.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Reasoning from a theory or proposition toward testable expectations.
concepts.example: A model predicts a relationship that a study then investigates.
concepts.false: A predicted relationship is true simply because a theory predicts it.
concepts.note: Evidence can challenge predictions as well as support them.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Collection and comparison of complementary components within a coordinated phase.
concepts.example: Survey findings and interviews are integrated around common research questions.
concepts.false: Convergent research requires ignoring disagreement between components.
concepts.note: Divergence can reveal context, measurement or sampling differences worth investigating.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A quantitative phase followed by qualitative inquiry to explain its findings.
concepts.example: Interviews explore why one clinic's numerical satisfaction scores were unusually low.
concepts.false: Explanatory sequential work always begins with qualitative tool development.
concepts.note: The explanatory purpose links the second phase to the first results.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Qualitative exploration followed by quantitative development or testing.
concepts.example: Interviews inform a questionnaire that is subsequently evaluated.
concepts.false: Exploratory sequential work begins by treating a final questionnaire as already complete.
concepts.note: Initial interpretation can shape later constructs, measures and hypotheses.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A conclusion developed through integration across study components.
concepts.example: Numerical uptake patterns and interview barriers jointly explain service access.
concepts.false: Meta-inference means reporting two disconnected result sections without interpretation.
concepts.note: Explain what the combined evidence adds beyond either component alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An intervention comparison assigning participants or clusters by a random process.
concepts.example: Eligible participants are randomly allocated to two therapy formats.
concepts.false: Random assignment guarantees identical baseline characteristics in every small trial.
concepts.note: Randomization balances groups in expectation; chance imbalance can still occur.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A group providing an alternative condition against which an intervention is evaluated.
concepts.example: One group receives an established active therapy rather than the new format.
concepts.false: Every comparison group must receive no support of any kind.
concepts.note: Usual care, active alternatives and other justified comparators are possible.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An intervention evaluation lacking random assignment in the relevant comparison.
concepts.example: Existing therapy groups receive different programmes.
concepts.false: Calling a study quasi-experimental removes all concern about confounding.
concepts.note: Alternative explanations require explicit design and analytical attention.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Repeated measurement with planned phase changes supporting within-case inference.
concepts.example: Treatment begins at different planned times across participants.
concepts.false: Any descriptive report about one client is automatically a controlled experiment.
concepts.note: Demonstration of experimental control distinguishes it from an ordinary case report.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Repeated observation before the relevant intervention phase.
concepts.example: Several probes document stable performance before treatment begins.
concepts.false: A single baseline value always establishes a stable trajectory.
concepts.note: Multiple observations help assess trend and variability before interpreting change.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Staggered intervention introduction across participants, behaviours or settings.
concepts.example: Three participants begin therapy after different baseline lengths.
concepts.false: Multiple baseline requires withdrawing an effective treatment in every case.
concepts.note: Staggered replication can test change without relying on withdrawal.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An intensive investigation of a bounded case or context.
concepts.example: Detailed records examine one individual's communication and service history.
concepts.false: A case study necessarily establishes a treatment's causal effect.
concepts.note: A case study can generate insight without experimental control.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Systematic collection of information from respondents about characteristics or experiences.
concepts.example: SLPs complete a structured questionnaire on service barriers.
concepts.false: A survey must always sample thousands of people to qualify as research.
concepts.note: Sampling, questions and response patterns determine what can be inferred.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Observation of variables within a defined time window without individual follow-up for change.
concepts.example: Researchers compare age groups during one school term.
concepts.false: Age-group differences prove how each individual child develops over time.
concepts.note: Cohort differences and confounding can complicate developmental interpretations.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Repeated observation of participants or units across time.
concepts.example: The same children complete language assessments on three occasions.
concepts.false: Following people over time automatically eliminates every causal ambiguity.
concepts.note: Temporal order helps, but confounding, measurement and attrition still matter.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Investigation of association without assigning the relevant exposure or predictor.
concepts.example: Family education and vocabulary are measured rather than experimentally assigned.
concepts.false: Correlation alone establishes that one variable causes the other.
concepts.note: Confounding and reverse direction remain possible explanations.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Inquiry using information about events already occurring before study initiation.
concepts.example: Records of earlier assessment and outcomes are reviewed.
concepts.false: Retrospective studies cannot contain quantitative measurements.
concepts.note: Historical data can be numerical but may have incomplete or inconsistent recording.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Planning measurement of events or outcomes as follow-up unfolds.
concepts.example: A newly enrolled group is assessed during the next year.
concepts.false: Prospective follow-up necessarily means random treatment assignment.
concepts.note: Time direction and allocation mechanism are different design dimensions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Follow-up of a defined group to investigate outcomes and exposures.
concepts.example: A birth cohort is followed for later language outcomes.
concepts.false: A cohort must consist only of people receiving one experimental treatment.
concepts.note: Cohorts can be defined by birth period, setting or other characteristics.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A design selecting outcome-defined cases and controls to compare prior exposures.
concepts.example: Children with and without an outcome are compared on earlier documented factors.
concepts.false: Case-control studies select groups solely by randomized therapy assignment.
concepts.note: Selection by outcome distinguishes case-control logic from exposure-defined follow-up.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Statistical combination of sufficiently compatible effect estimates from multiple studies.
concepts.example: Comparable trials contribute estimates to a pooled analysis.
concepts.false: Any review containing several papers is automatically a meta-analysis.
concepts.note: Pooling requires justified compatibility, appropriate models and attention to bias.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Credibility of conclusions about the relationship studied within a design.
concepts.example: A trial reduces alternative explanations through allocation and standardized assessment.
concepts.false: Internal validity means findings apply to every culture and service setting.
concepts.note: Applicability beyond the study is an external-validity question.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The extent to which inferences apply to relevant populations and settings beyond the study.
concepts.example: A reader considers fit for Urdu-speaking clients in a local clinic.
concepts.false: A tightly controlled study automatically generalizes everywhere.
concepts.note: Assess the match between study participants, procedures and intended use.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Preventing advance knowledge of upcoming treatment assignments during enrolment.
concepts.example: Recruiters cannot predict which group the next eligible participant will enter.
concepts.false: Allocation concealment is identical to hiding results from participants after testing.
concepts.note: Concealment protects the allocation process; blinding concerns knowledge after allocation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Keeping outcome assessors unaware of relevant group assignments where feasible.
concepts.example: A rater evaluates coded speech samples without knowing treatment group.
concepts.false: Blinding an assessor always guarantees that recruitment was random.
concepts.note: Blinding and randomization address different sources of bias.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Loss of participants or observations during study follow-up.
concepts.example: More participants leave one intervention arm before the final assessment.
concepts.false: Dropout is harmless whenever the initial sample was large.
concepts.note: Differential or outcome-related loss can bias the comparison.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The extent to which an intervention is delivered as specified.
concepts.example: Session checks document whether planned procedures and dosage were implemented.
concepts.false: Naming a programme proves it was implemented consistently.
concepts.note: Fidelity helps distinguish the intervention plan from what actually occurred.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Repeating an investigation to examine the robustness of a finding.
concepts.example: Another team tests the same intervention logic in a different setting.
concepts.false: A study is worthless simply because an earlier study asked a similar question.
concepts.note: Justified replication can test reliability, context and boundary conditions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#2 Types of research (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A characteristic that can differ across units, conditions or time.
concepts.example: Participants differ in age and vocabulary score.
concepts.false: A characteristic is a variable only when experimentally manipulated.
concepts.note: Variables can be measured, classified or manipulated depending on the design.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A theoretically meaningful concept represented through observations or indicators.
concepts.example: Communication participation is represented through a specified measure.
concepts.false: A construct and one questionnaire item are necessarily identical.
concepts.note: A measure operationalizes a concept without exhausting every possible interpretation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An explanation of what a concept means in the study.
concepts.example: The protocol explains what it means by functional communication.
concepts.false: A conceptual definition is only a list of software commands.
concepts.note: Meaning should be clarified before selecting its measurement procedure.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A precise specification of how a variable is measured or manipulated.
concepts.example: Intelligibility is the percentage of target words transcribed correctly by specified listeners.
concepts.false: Saying that communication is good provides a reproducible operational definition.
concepts.note: Specify procedures, units, timing and relevant scoring rules.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An assigned or explanatory factor examined in relation to an outcome.
concepts.example: In an experiment, two therapy-intensity conditions are assigned.
concepts.false: Every independent variable in every study has been randomized.
concepts.note: Observational predictors are not automatically manipulated causes.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The response or outcome measured in a specified analysis.
concepts.example: Correct target productions after training form the outcome.
concepts.false: The dependent variable is necessarily the treatment assigned by the researcher.
concepts.note: A variable's role depends on the research question and model.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A variable representing a proposed pathway linking a predictor to an outcome.
concepts.example: A programme may improve caregiver practice, which then relates to child outcomes.
concepts.false: A mediator can never be measured directly or through indicators.
concepts.note: Mechanisms can be measured; causal mediation requires stronger assumptions than association alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A variable associated with differences in a relationship across its levels.
concepts.example: Treatment effects are compared across age groups through an interaction.
concepts.false: A moderator must lie between treatment and outcome on a causal pathway.
concepts.note: Moderation asks when or for whom a relationship differs, unlike mediation's pathway question.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A factor deliberately held constant or addressed analytically in a study.
concepts.example: Testing instructions are standardized across participants.
concepts.false: Controlling one factor eliminates all threats to validity.
concepts.note: State what was controlled and how; residual problems may remain.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A factor creating an alternative explanation through its relationship with exposure and outcome.
concepts.example: Initial severity differs by chosen treatment and predicts later scores.
concepts.false: Any variable measured after treatment is automatically a safe confounder to adjust for.
concepts.note: Adjustment needs a justified model; indiscriminate control can introduce bias.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A variable included in an analytical model alongside factors of primary interest.
concepts.example: Baseline score is included in an outcome model.
concepts.false: A covariate is guaranteed to be a cause merely because it appears in a regression.
concepts.note: Covariate is a model-role label, not proof of a causal relationship.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Variation from factors outside the primary relationship being investigated.
concepts.example: Different testing environments contribute unrelated score fluctuation.
concepts.false: Every extraneous factor is necessarily a confounder.
concepts.note: Extraneous variation may add noise without systematically distorting the focal relationship.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Categories without an inherent quantitative order.
concepts.example: Diagnostic categories are coded 1, 2 and 3 for identification.
concepts.false: Coding categories with numbers makes their arithmetic mean clinically meaningful.
concepts.note: Numeric labels identify groups; frequencies and appropriate categorical analyses remain possible.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Ordered categories whose numerical distances are not established as equal.
concepts.example: Mild, moderate, severe and profound ratings are ranked.
concepts.false: The difference between adjacent severity categories must always be identical.
concepts.note: Order is justified while equal intervals require additional evidence.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Equal-interval measurement without a meaningful absolute zero.
concepts.example: Celsius temperature permits meaningful differences but not simple temperature ratios.
concepts.false: Forty degrees Celsius is twice as hot as twenty by a valid scale ratio.
concepts.note: Absence of a true zero prevents that direct ratio interpretation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Equal-interval measurement with a meaningful zero supporting ratios.
concepts.example: A 200-millisecond duration is twice a 100-millisecond duration.
concepts.false: All numerical test scores are necessarily ratio-scale measures of ability.
concepts.note: The property concerns the measurement scale, not the presence of printed numbers.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A logarithmic representation relative to a specified reference.
concepts.example: Sound level is reported in dB relative to a reference intensity.
concepts.false: A value of 0 dB necessarily means complete physical absence of sound.
concepts.note: Underlying physical intensity and its logarithmic dB expression have different arithmetic properties.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A numerical variable taking separate countable values in its specified form.
concepts.example: An assessment counts the number of errors in a fixed task.
concepts.false: An error count must include every fractional real number between zero and one.
concepts.note: Counts differ from continuous measurements even when both use numbers.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A variable conceptually varying along a continuum within a range.
concepts.example: Response duration can vary by fractions of a second.
concepts.false: Rounding a recorded duration proves the underlying quantity is categorical.
concepts.note: Recording precision and the conceptual nature of the quantity are distinct.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Consistency or precision of measurement under specified conditions.
concepts.example: Independent raters produce similar scores from the same speech samples.
concepts.false: A highly consistent measure must measure the intended construct validly.
concepts.note: Consistency alone does not establish the appropriateness of an interpretation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Support for the intended interpretation and use of scores.
concepts.example: Evidence is examined for using a measure with the target language group.
concepts.false: A test valid for one purpose is automatically valid for every population and use.
concepts.note: Validation concerns particular interpretations, populations and decisions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Consistency or agreement across raters under a specified scoring procedure.
concepts.example: Two trained raters score the same recorded samples.
concepts.false: Rater agreement is assessed by comparing completely unrelated tasks.
concepts.note: Match the reliability or agreement statistic to scale and purpose.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Stability of measurements across occasions when the target is expected to remain stable.
concepts.example: A stable skill is assessed twice under comparable conditions.
concepts.false: True therapeutic change must be counted as measurement unreliability.
concepts.note: Expected change and measurement error must be distinguished when evaluating stability.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A measure's capacity to detect relevant change in the construct.
concepts.example: A probe captures small gains over a treatment interval.
concepts.false: A strong diagnostic classification tool is automatically sensitive to short-term change.
concepts.note: Suitability for diagnosis does not ensure responsiveness as an outcome measure.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Characteristics describing participants' backgrounds.
concepts.example: Age, education and language history are recorded.
concepts.false: A demographic label determines every individual's ability without further evidence.
concepts.note: Group descriptors do not justify stereotypes or deterministic conclusions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Indicators of articulation, fluency, voice or related speech behaviours.
concepts.example: A specified speech task supplies accuracy and disfluency counts.
concepts.false: A speech measure needs no description of task or scoring rules.
concepts.note: Task, unit, sampling window and scoring affect interpretation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Indicators of comprehension or production across linguistic domains.
concepts.example: A narrative task records defined grammatical and discourse outcomes.
concepts.false: One vocabulary score exhaustively measures every aspect of language.
concepts.note: Language is multidimensional; choose outcomes aligned with the question.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Processing and manipulation of speech-sound information.
concepts.example: A task asks a participant to delete an initial phoneme.
concepts.false: Phonological processing is identical to naming written font types.
concepts.note: Sound-based tasks require attention to language and task demands.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Higher-order regulation such as inhibition, shifting and goal-directed control.
concepts.example: A study examines switching demands during a communication task.
concepts.false: Executive function refers only to how loudly a person speaks.
concepts.note: Define the particular component rather than treating the label as one simple score.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Temporary maintenance and manipulation of information.
concepts.example: A task requires retaining verbal material while processing it.
concepts.false: Working memory is identical to a lifetime store of vocabulary definitions.
concepts.note: Distinguish short-term processing demands from long-term lexical knowledge.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The rate at which specified information is processed or responses are produced.
concepts.example: Word-recognition latency is measured in milliseconds.
concepts.false: Faster responses always prove greater accuracy on every task.
concepts.note: Speed and accuracy can trade off; task conditions matter.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Characteristics of sensory access or processing relevant to the task.
concepts.example: Hearing access and visual support are considered in assessment design.
concepts.false: Normal peripheral hearing proves every auditory-processing task is unaffected.
concepts.note: Sensory access, processing and task performance are related but not identical.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Assessment attentive to language history, norms and the intended interpretation.
concepts.example: An English measure is evaluated before use with Urdu-speaking participants.
concepts.false: A linguistic difference from English is sufficient evidence of disorder.
concepts.note: Cultural and linguistic fit must be considered to avoid misinterpretation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Initial learning of a targeted skill during intervention.
concepts.example: A child improves on trained words within sessions.
concepts.false: Improvement on trained material proves transfer to every untrained setting.
concepts.note: Acquisition is distinct from generalization beyond the training context.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Transfer to untrained items, contexts or communication partners.
concepts.example: Newly learned productions occur in untreated conversation samples.
concepts.false: Generalization is established only by repeating the same trained list.
concepts.note: Include untrained material or relevant new contexts in the measurement plan.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Retention of gains over time beyond the relevant intervention phase.
concepts.example: Follow-up probes examine whether learned skills persist.
concepts.false: A posttest immediately after treatment establishes long-term maintenance.
concepts.note: Specify the follow-up interval and subsequent intervention exposure.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Co-occurrence of additional conditions that may affect interpretation or participation.
concepts.example: A study records relevant co-occurring attention or hearing conditions.
concepts.false: All individuals with one diagnosis have identical co-occurring conditions.
concepts.note: Report relevant heterogeneity without assuming a universal profile.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Age- or experience-related characteristics relevant to change and measurement.
concepts.example: Researchers consider age and prior language-learning opportunities.
concepts.false: Every child must reach every language milestone on one exact day.
concepts.note: Development varies; age ranges are guides rather than deterministic diagnostic rules.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Values not observed for measurements planned in a study.
concepts.example: Some participants miss the final language assessment.
concepts.false: Replacing every missing outcome with zero is always an unbiased solution.
concepts.note: The reasons and analytical handling of missingness affect interpretation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Difference or uncertainty arising from imperfect observation of a quantity.
concepts.example: Small score fluctuations reflect rater or task variability around stable ability.
concepts.false: Every observed score difference necessarily reflects true developmental change.
concepts.note: Assess error relative to the size and purpose of the change being interpreted.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Definitions and Variables (1).pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The group to which the research aims to relate its conclusions.
concepts.example: A study targets primary schoolchildren in a defined district.
concepts.false: The target population is necessarily identical to everyone attending one clinic.
concepts.note: Define intended scope before deciding how recruitment will occur.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Members practically reachable through the study's setting and procedures.
concepts.example: Participating schools provide the accessible pool.
concepts.false: Accessibility by itself establishes complete coverage of the target population.
concepts.note: Distinguish the intended population from those available through recruitment.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Units actually selected or participating in a study.
concepts.example: One hundred eligible children contribute observations.
concepts.false: A sample is always every member of the intended population.
concepts.note: A subset may or may not adequately represent the intended target.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The operational list or structure from which selection is made.
concepts.example: A school enrolment list supplies the frame.
concepts.false: A frame is guaranteed to contain every eligible person without omissions.
concepts.note: Undercoverage, duplicates and outdated entries can affect selection.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An attempt to study every member of a defined population.
concepts.example: All eligible employees in a small service are invited and assessed.
concepts.false: Studying most eligible members is automatically a complete census.
concepts.note: Coverage and nonresponse still need documentation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Selection using a random mechanism with known nonzero inclusion probabilities.
concepts.example: Listed eligible members enter a specified random selection procedure.
concepts.false: Every probability method requires equal probabilities for all members.
concepts.note: Known probabilities can differ across strata or stages.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Random selection giving each possible fixed-size subset equal probability in the standard definition.
concepts.example: A random generator selects unique IDs from a complete list.
concepts.false: Interviewing whoever volunteers first is simple random sampling.
concepts.note: A specified chance mechanism distinguishes random selection from casual choice.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Selection at a fixed interval after an appropriate random start.
concepts.example: From 300 names, a random start precedes selection of every twentieth.
concepts.false: Choosing every twentieth without considering the start and ordering removes all bias risks.
concepts.note: Periodicity in the frame can compromise the intended sampling properties.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The spacing used in a systematic design, commonly based on population divided by sample size.
concepts.example: Three hundred divided by fifteen gives an interval of twenty.
concepts.false: The interval for 300 names and 15 selections is necessarily fifteen.
concepts.note: Describe the actual procedure when ratios are not integers or frames are complex.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Partitioning into strata and randomly selecting within each stratum.
concepts.example: Students are randomly sampled separately within each academic year.
concepts.false: Setting group quotas without random within-group selection guarantees stratified random sampling.
concepts.note: Random selection within strata distinguishes this design from ordinary quota recruitment.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Assigning stratum sample sizes in proportion to population shares.
concepts.example: A group containing 40% of the population supplies 40% of selections.
concepts.false: Proportional allocation requires equal numbers from unequal-size strata.
concepts.note: Multiply total intended sample by the stratum's population proportion.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Selecting strata at unequal sampling fractions for a stated purpose.
concepts.example: A small subgroup is oversampled to support subgroup analysis.
concepts.false: Oversampling a subgroup necessarily invalidates every possible population estimate.
concepts.note: Appropriate weights and design-aware analysis can address unequal selection.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A defined subgroup from which participants are separately selected in a stratified design.
concepts.example: Academic year defines the strata in a student survey.
concepts.false: A stratum is defined as one randomly chosen entire school in a cluster sample.
concepts.note: Strata and clusters serve different roles in the sampling plan.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A naturally or operationally grouped set of units used in cluster sampling.
concepts.example: Schools act as clusters of pupils.
concepts.false: Every real cluster must perfectly reproduce the whole population's composition.
concepts.note: Mini-population is a teaching analogy, not a guaranteed feature of actual clusters.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Random selection of groups followed by study of units in those selected groups.
concepts.example: Twenty schools are selected from a district's school list.
concepts.false: Ordinary cluster sampling always selects individuals from every single school.
concepts.note: Sampling some clusters distinguishes it from sampling within every stratum.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Selection of clusters followed by inclusion of all eligible units within them.
concepts.example: All eligible pupils in selected schools are assessed.
concepts.false: One-stage cluster sampling requires a further random sample of pupils within every selected school.
concepts.note: Further within-cluster selection creates an additional stage.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Selection through linked stages, such as areas, schools and pupils.
concepts.example: Schools are selected first and children sampled within them.
concepts.false: Multistage sampling means repeating the same questionnaire after therapy.
concepts.note: Stages concern selection levels rather than measurement occasions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Recruitment primarily based on accessibility and availability.
concepts.example: The available clients at one nearby clinic are invited.
concepts.false: A convenience sample becomes random merely because participants have different ages.
concepts.note: Diversity alone does not establish a probability selection mechanism.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Deliberate selection of information-rich cases meeting a study's purpose.
concepts.example: Caregivers with relevant service experience are selected for interviews.
concepts.false: Researcher judgment guarantees minimal error and population representativeness.
concepts.note: Justify why selected experiences illuminate the question and acknowledge limits.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Inclusion of every eligible accessible case encountered over a defined period until a stated endpoint.
concepts.example: All qualifying clinic referrals during six months are invited.
concepts.false: Consecutive sampling means moving between arbitrary groups only after each is analyzed.
concepts.note: Consecutive inclusion requires a defined recruitment stream and consistent eligibility rules.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Nonprobability recruitment until specified subgroup numbers are filled.
concepts.example: Researchers recruit until each diagnosis quota is reached.
concepts.false: Matching subgroup proportions establishes random selection within those groups.
concepts.note: Quotas can control composition without removing within-group selection bias.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Chain-referral recruitment through participants' networks.
concepts.example: Initial participants suggest other eligible people with a rare condition.
concepts.false: Snowball sampling gives every unknown population member a known equal chance.
concepts.note: Network dependence and initial contacts can shape who becomes reachable.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Conditions defining eligibility for participation.
concepts.example: Age range and language background are specified before enrolment.
concepts.false: Inclusion criteria may be changed secretly to obtain a preferred result.
concepts.note: Criteria should match the question and be applied transparently.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Specified reasons an otherwise relevant person is not included.
concepts.example: A safety-related condition excludes an individual from one protocol.
concepts.false: Exclusions require no ethical or scientific justification.
concepts.note: Avoid unjustified restrictions and report their implications for applicability.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Systematic distortion caused by how a sample differs from its target.
concepts.example: Recruitment excludes families unable to attend during working hours.
concepts.false: Increasing sample size always eliminates systematic selection bias.
concepts.note: More biased observations can produce a more precise biased estimate.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Random variation of sample estimates across repeated probability samples.
concepts.example: Two valid random samples give slightly different prevalence estimates.
concepts.false: Sampling error is identical to deliberately selecting only favourable cases.
concepts.note: Chance variability differs from systematic selection distortion.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Distortion when response is related to characteristics important to the research.
concepts.example: Families facing the greatest barriers are less likely to return a survey.
concepts.false: A high invitation count guarantees absence of nonresponse bias.
concepts.note: Evaluate who responded and why nonresponse could matter.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A distinction between selecting a sample and allocating enrolled units to conditions.
concepts.example: Convenience recruits are randomly assigned to two treatment groups.
concepts.false: Random treatment allocation proves that recruitment represented the whole population.
concepts.note: Allocation can improve internal comparisons without fixing population sampling.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Justifying numbers from precision, effect, design, variability and feasibility.
concepts.example: An estimate allows for clustering and expected loss to follow-up.
concepts.false: Every study needs exactly thirty participants regardless of its question.
concepts.note: No universal number replaces design-specific justification.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Clear reporting of who was eligible, approached, enrolled and analyzed.
concepts.example: A recruitment account explains exclusions and refusals.
concepts.false: Reporting only the final number fully explains the recruitment process.
concepts.note: Transparent selection allows readers to judge applicability and potential bias.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Sampling_Methods.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An explicit inquiry narrow enough to investigate with suitable evidence.
concepts.example: A question specifies a population, intervention comparison and vocabulary outcome.
concepts.false: A broad topic label alone fully specifies an answerable study.
concepts.note: Clarify what is unknown, for whom, and what evidence could answer it.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An experience-based starting point that may generate an investigable question.
concepts.example: A clinician notices variable attendance across service formats.
concepts.false: One observed improvement proves general treatment superiority.
concepts.note: Observation motivates investigation without substituting for an appropriate comparison.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Narrowing a broad interest into a manageable inquiry.
concepts.example: Therapy and language becomes a comparison of defined programmes in one population.
concepts.false: Refinement requires hiding eligibility criteria until after seeing results.
concepts.note: Set boundaries to align the question, methods and feasible scope.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An evidence-supported uncertainty or limitation motivating further work.
concepts.example: A review finds conflicting results for a clearly defined outcome.
concepts.false: Any topic not personally encountered by the student is automatically an established gap.
concepts.note: A gap must be justified through relevant searching and appraisal.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Stating who the question concerns through relevant characteristics.
concepts.example: Age range, diagnosis and language history define the group of interest.
