concepts.false: Diagnosis alone always supplies every eligibility detail needed.
concepts.note: Include characteristics necessary to interpret the question without arbitrary overrestriction.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Clear description of the programme, delivery and dosage being investigated.
concepts.example: A protocol states session frequency, duration and parent-coaching procedures.
concepts.false: Giving an intervention a fashionable name makes dosage irrelevant.
concepts.note: The assigned procedure must be sufficiently defined for interpretation and replication.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Selection of the alternative relevant to the question and ethical context.
concepts.example: New treatment is compared with usual care rather than an unrelated group.
concepts.false: A comparator must always be a group of typically developing people.
concepts.note: Active alternatives and usual care answer different questions from no treatment.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Defining what result is examined and how it will be measured.
concepts.example: Everyday intelligibility is assessed by a specified listener protocol.
concepts.false: Any available test score answers every communication-related question.
concepts.note: Outcome choice must match the construct and the proposed intervention target.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Stating relevant intervention, measurement or follow-up intervals.
concepts.example: Outcomes are measured after eight weeks and at later follow-up.
concepts.false: Post-treatment timing can never affect interpretation of an intervention.
concepts.note: Immediate acquisition and later maintenance require different measurement occasions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Inquiry about characteristics, frequency or distribution.
concepts.example: What service barriers are reported in the selected clinics?
concepts.false: Every descriptive question requires random assignment to therapy.
concepts.note: Description and causal attribution require different forms of evidence.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Inquiry about a relationship between measured factors.
concepts.example: Is home-language exposure associated with a specified vocabulary measure?
concepts.false: Including the word association guarantees proof of direction of causation.
concepts.note: Interpret measured relationships in light of design and alternative explanations.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Inquiry about effects attributable to a specified intervention or exposure.
concepts.example: Would assigning one service format change a defined outcome?
concepts.false: A causal-sounding sentence makes an uncontrolled design causally conclusive.
concepts.note: The design and assumptions must support the effect being asked about.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Inquiry about meaning and lived or reported experience.
concepts.example: How do adults who stutter describe workplace participation?
concepts.false: Every experience question must be answered by comparing numerical group means.
concepts.note: Qualitative approaches can address meaning without forcing it into a treatment-effect format.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Matching the kind of inquiry with an appropriate strategy for evidence.
concepts.example: A question about experience leads to contextualized interviews and interpretation.
concepts.false: Choosing a favourite statistical test should always precede defining the research question.
concepts.note: Question, evidence, design and analysis should form a coherent chain.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Selecting observations that actually address the question's construct.
concepts.example: A functional communication question uses an outcome reflecting everyday communication.
concepts.false: Naming an outcome scale proves it measures every intended construct.
concepts.note: Check the intended interpretation and responsiveness of the chosen score.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Recruitment that supplies evidence from the people or cases relevant to the inquiry.
concepts.example: A caregiver-experience study recruits people with the relevant experience.
concepts.false: A large unrelated sample answers a narrowly defined target-population question.
concepts.note: Relevance of the sampled cases matters alongside numbers.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Limits consistent with accessible participants, resources and time.
concepts.example: A student restricts a proposal to procedures available locally.
concepts.false: An impossible recruitment plan is rescued merely by an impressive title.
concepts.note: Refine scope transparently rather than promising unachievable coverage.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An inquiry that can be investigated without unjustified harm or coercion.
concepts.example: A comparison preserves appropriate usual services and voluntary participation.
concepts.false: Important scientific uncertainty always permits withholding essential care without justification.
concepts.note: The question's value does not override participant protection.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The main outcome prespecified for a study's central inference.
concepts.example: One vocabulary outcome anchors the trial's sample-size calculation.
concepts.false: A primary outcome may be selected secretly after whichever result has the smallest p value.
concepts.note: Prespecification helps limit selective outcome reporting.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An additional outcome answering a supplementary question.
concepts.example: Participation is measured alongside the main target-skill outcome.
concepts.false: A secondary outcome must be ignored and omitted from the report.
concepts.note: Report planned outcomes with appropriate interpretation of multiplicity and priority.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A prediction specifying the direction of a relationship or difference.
concepts.example: The new format is predicted to increase a prespecified outcome.
concepts.false: Every quantitative hypothesis must avoid stating a direction.
concepts.note: A prediction should be justified and distinguished from the observed result.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A specified reference hypothesis for statistical testing.
concepts.example: The model posits no mean difference between conditions.
concepts.false: Failing to reject the null proves exact equality of every relevant effect.
concepts.note: Lack of evidence against a null is not automatic evidence of equivalence.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A justified planning value for the magnitude of a target difference or relationship.
concepts.example: Sample-size planning uses a difference considered substantively important.
concepts.false: Smaller target effects always require fewer observations under otherwise fixed conditions.
concepts.note: Smaller effects generally require more information for comparable power.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Limited access to eligible participants requiring realistic design choices.
concepts.example: A rare-condition study considers repeated-measure or multicentre options.
concepts.false: A rare population licenses inventing participants to reach a target number.
concepts.note: Adapt the question and design honestly to recruitment realities.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Avoiding substitution of a structural or diagnostic construct for a behavioural treatment target.
concepts.example: A speech-coaching study distinguishes intelligibility from structural velopharyngeal function.
concepts.false: Improvement in speech practice automatically proves correction of an anatomical deficit.
concepts.note: Specify what the intervention can plausibly target and measure that construct appropriately.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec #5 Research-Questions-in-Speech-Language-Pathology.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A mnemonic organizing the components of a researchable inquiry.
concepts.example: A student separates people, treatment, comparison and outcome.
concepts.false: Selecting a framework automatically validates a study's design or conclusion.
concepts.note: Frameworks clarify components; they do not replace methodological judgment.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Population, Intervention, Comparison and Outcome for a focused intervention question.
concepts.example: Two therapy formats are compared for a defined group and outcome.
concepts.false: The O in PICO means the person observing the test.
concepts.note: The letters identify components, not a mandatory experimental design by themselves.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The people or problem targeted by an intervention question.
concepts.example: School-age children with persistent speech sound difficulties form P.
concepts.false: P in PICO is always the professional delivering treatment.
concepts.note: Relevant participant characteristics define the target group.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The treatment, programme or assigned procedure being evaluated.
concepts.example: Ultrasound biofeedback is the intervention in a comparison question.
concepts.false: Intervention in PICO means the outcome score obtained afterwards.
concepts.note: Describe the procedure separately from the results it is intended to influence.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The alternative condition used to interpret the intervention.
concepts.example: Traditional articulation therapy provides the comparison format.
concepts.false: Comparison in PICO necessarily means a different outcome instrument.
concepts.note: Different conditions should be measured on interpretable outcome bases.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The result or construct examined in the intervention question.
concepts.example: Accuracy on a prespecified speech task is the outcome.
concepts.false: A broad aspiration such as better life needs no operational clarification.
concepts.note: Specify the construct and measurement rather than assuming an intention is a measure.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: PICO expanded with an explicit time element.
concepts.example: A question adds outcomes after ten weeks of treatment.
concepts.false: Adding T establishes that treatment assignment was randomized.
concepts.note: Time clarifies the intended interval without establishing allocation method.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Population, Exposure and Outcome for exposure-focused or related questions.
concepts.example: Screen-time exposure is related to a defined language outcome without assignment.
concepts.false: PEO requires researchers to assign every naturally occurring exposure.
concepts.note: Its components support observational questions but do not prove causal effects.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Population, Exposure, Comparator and Outcome.
concepts.example: Higher and lower measured exposure groups are compared on one outcome.
concepts.false: The exposure must always be an experimentally assigned therapeutic programme.
concepts.note: Distinguish exposure comparisons from intervention assignment.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A factor or experience encountered rather than necessarily assigned.
concepts.example: Naturally occurring home-language environments are documented.
concepts.false: Calling a factor exposure proves it was measured before the outcome.
concepts.note: Establish time order and measurement separately from the label.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Population, Concept and Context for framing a scoping inquiry.
concepts.example: Evidence on telepractice for adults with aphasia is mapped across community settings.
concepts.false: Both C letters in PCC mean comparison groups.
concepts.note: In this framework the C components are concept and context.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The central idea, phenomenon, intervention or measure being mapped.
concepts.example: Communication-participation measures form the concept in a scoping review.
concepts.false: Concept in PCC must always be a randomized placebo.
concepts.note: A scoping concept can encompass types of evidence or service practice.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The setting, geographical or sociocultural circumstances defining a scoping inquiry.
concepts.example: South Asian community services provide the review context.
concepts.false: Context and sample size are identical components.
concepts.note: Define relevant environmental boundaries rather than confusing them with participant count.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Sample, Phenomenon of Interest, Design, Evaluation and Research type.
concepts.example: Caregiver experience is explored through interviews within a qualitative inquiry.
concepts.false: SPIDER was created solely to replace every quantitative intervention framework.
concepts.note: It supports qualitative or mixed evidence questions; suitability depends on the purpose.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The group whose relevant experience or perspective is investigated.
concepts.example: Parents of children receiving a service form the sample element.
concepts.false: S in SPIDER always means the physical clinic setting.
concepts.note: Do not transfer the S definition from SPICE to SPIDER.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The experience, behaviour or process explored in a SPIDER question.
concepts.example: Navigating telepractice barriers is the phenomenon of interest.
concepts.false: A phenomenon of interest must always be a randomized drug dose.
concepts.note: Experience-focused inquiry does not require an assigned intervention.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The proposed evidence-generating procedure or study form in this mnemonic.
concepts.example: Semi-structured interviews specify D in a teaching example.
concepts.false: D in SPIDER identifies the final clinical diagnosis alone.
concepts.note: Framework terminology is pragmatic; still distinguish collection procedure from broader methodology.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Views, experiences, attitudes or other evaluative material being examined.
concepts.example: Parent perceptions of access difficulties specify evaluation.
concepts.false: Evaluation in SPIDER must always be a standardized test score.
concepts.note: Evaluation can capture subjective meaning relevant to the research question.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The broad inquiry type represented by R in the framework.
concepts.example: A study is explicitly identified as qualitative.
concepts.false: The R in SPIDER always means the recruitment response rate.
concepts.note: State the inquiry type rather than confusing it with an outcome or statistic.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Setting, Perspective, Intervention or Interest, Comparison and Evaluation.
concepts.example: A service question compares group and individual therapy from clients' perspectives.
concepts.false: SPICE stands for Sample, Programme, Instrument, Cost and Experiment.
concepts.note: The corrected mapping distinguishes service setting and stakeholder perspective.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The service or physical context where a SPICE question is situated.
concepts.example: Outpatient hospital clinics supply S.
concepts.false: S in SPICE necessarily identifies the sample rather than the setting.
concepts.note: Keep framework-specific meanings separate even when initial letters match.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The stakeholder viewpoint central to a service question.
concepts.example: Adults with aphasia provide the perspective on communication confidence.
concepts.false: P in SPICE is always the posttest date.
concepts.note: Stakeholder perspective differs from the location of the service.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The alternative service and criterion for evaluating it in the mnemonic.
concepts.example: Individual therapy is compared with group therapy on confidence.
concepts.false: Comparison and evaluation are interchangeable labels for one element.
concepts.note: Identify what is contrasted separately from the criterion used to judge it.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Expectation, Client group, Location, Impact, Professionals and Service.
concepts.example: A service-improvement question identifies goals, users, setting, staff and provision.
concepts.false: ECLIPSE is a statistical test for normally distributed gain scores.
concepts.note: This is a question-structuring tool for service or management issues.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The improvement or information sought through the service inquiry.
concepts.example: Improving the screening pathway states the expectation.
concepts.false: Expectation in ECLIPSE proves that improvement already occurred.
concepts.note: A desired improvement is an inquiry goal, not an observed finding.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The users of the service and the place it is delivered.
concepts.example: Stroke patients and acute wards specify client group and location.
concepts.false: Client group in ECLIPSE means only the staff delivering the service.
concepts.note: Professionals and client group have distinct roles in this framework.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The intended difference or consequence of service improvement.
concepts.example: Reduced service delay is the proposed impact.
concepts.false: Impact is identical to the name of the professional team.
concepts.note: State the intended effect separately from staffing and service identity.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The staff involved and the service being investigated.
concepts.example: Nurses and SLPs deliver a specified screening pathway.
concepts.false: SE in ECLIPSE is the abbreviation for standard error.
concepts.note: SE denotes Service in this mnemonic, not a statistical quantity.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Matching a mnemonic's emphasis to the substantive inquiry.
concepts.example: An evidence-mapping question uses PCC rather than forcing a therapy comparator.
concepts.false: Every research question must use PICO regardless of its purpose.
concepts.note: Choose for fit, while recognizing that frameworks are aids rather than exclusive laws.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The distinction between structuring a question and constructing a retrieval query.
concepts.example: A PICO question is translated into selected search concept blocks.
concepts.false: Every PICO element must always be searched with AND in every database.
concepts.note: Overly restrictive outcome or comparison blocks can miss relevant evidence.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Research_Questions_SLP_Frameworks.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Critical, organized synthesis of existing scholarship relevant to an inquiry.
concepts.example: A chapter explains agreements, disagreements and methodological limits across studies.
concepts.false: A literature review is complete when titles are listed without interpretation.
concepts.note: Synthesis connects sources to a question rather than merely accumulating citations.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A group of related terms representing one searchable concept.
concepts.example: Alternative names for an intervention are grouped together.
concepts.false: One concept block should always combine unrelated populations and outcomes with OR.
concepts.note: Organize synonyms within concepts before combining different concepts.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A free-text term used to retrieve potentially relevant records.
concepts.example: A search includes telepractice as a title or abstract term.
concepts.false: A single keyword guarantees retrieval of every relevant paper.
concepts.note: Include justified variants and complementary indexing terms.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An alternative expression used to improve retrieval for a concept.
concepts.example: Telepractice and teletherapy are considered as alternative search expressions.
concepts.false: All clinically distinct disorders must be treated as exact synonyms in a search.
concepts.note: Retrieval expansion does not establish conceptual interchangeability.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An intersection operator requiring records to meet combined concepts.
concepts.example: Stuttering AND intervention asks for both concept conditions.
concepts.false: AND normally broadens a fixed database search by accepting either concept.
concepts.note: AND typically narrows relative to either component searched alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A union operator retrieving records meeting either or both alternatives.
concepts.example: Aphasia OR dysphasia retrieves either specified term.
concepts.false: OR means a record containing both alternatives must be excluded.
concepts.note: Boolean OR is ordinarily inclusive rather than exclusive.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An exclusion operator removing records that meet a specified condition.
concepts.example: A carefully justified exclusion removes a clearly irrelevant concept.
concepts.false: NOT can never remove a relevant mixed-population study.
concepts.note: Exclusions may discard useful records and should be tested cautiously.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Grouping that makes the intended Boolean combinations explicit.
concepts.example: Two synonyms joined by OR are grouped before adding an AND block.
concepts.false: Parentheses are only decorative and never affect search logic.
concepts.note: Databases differ in precedence, so explicit grouping improves clarity.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Searching for words together in a specified phrase pattern.
concepts.example: A database query requests the phrase speech perception.
concepts.false: Quotation marks behave identically in every database and circumstance.
concepts.note: Verify platform-specific phrase rules and test whether relevant records are retrieved.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Use of a supported wildcard to retrieve word variants sharing a stem.
concepts.example: A supported child stem search retrieves relevant word endings.
concepts.false: The same truncation symbol and behaviour are guaranteed across all platforms.
concepts.note: Check the database's syntax, limits and effect on automatic mapping.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A standardized indexing system representing concepts consistently.
concepts.example: A database assigns a recognized subject heading to an indexed article.
concepts.false: Controlled vocabulary consists only of whichever spelling an author used in an abstract.
concepts.note: Index terms complement free-text searching rather than duplicating its exact mechanism.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Medical Subject Headings, the NLM controlled vocabulary used for MEDLINE indexing.
concepts.example: A PubMed search combines relevant MeSH headings with title-abstract terms.
concepts.false: Every new PubMed record necessarily has complete MeSH indexing immediately.
concepts.note: Indexing coverage and timing are reasons to combine headings with free text.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Organization of headings into broader and narrower relationships.
concepts.example: A researcher checks whether narrower headings are included by a search.
concepts.false: MeSH headings form only an unstructured alphabetical list with no conceptual relations.
concepts.note: Understand hierarchical expansion and inspect relevant indexing choices.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Retrieval restricted to specified bibliographic text fields under a platform's syntax.
concepts.example: PubMed uses a title-abstract tag to target text fields.
concepts.false: A title-abstract tag searches every word in every publisher's full article.
concepts.note: Field restrictions define where matching occurs, not full-text access.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An NLM search resource for biomedical citations, including MEDLINE and additional records.
concepts.example: A researcher searches biomedical communication-disorder literature.
concepts.false: Every PubMed citation provides free full text and complete MEDLINE indexing.
concepts.note: Citation discovery, indexing status and access to full text are separate matters.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Discipline-specific publications and evidence resources for communication sciences.
concepts.example: ASHA journals and evidence summaries inform a speech-language question.
concepts.false: A publisher search alone necessarily covers all worldwide SLP evidence.
concepts.note: Discipline focus is useful but does not replace broader, question-appropriate searching.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Resources serving domains such as rehabilitation, nursing, psychology and education.
concepts.example: CINAHL, PsycINFO or ERIC supplement a topic-specific search.
concepts.false: All databases cover exactly the same journals and disciplines.
concepts.note: Choose sources for the question and document their contribution.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Finding related evidence through cited or citing publications.
concepts.example: Reference lists and citing papers identify additional relevant studies.
concepts.false: Citation tracking guarantees identification of all relevant unpublished work.
concepts.note: Record supplementary discovery rather than assuming networks are complete.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Examining references cited by an identified publication.
concepts.example: A review's reference list points to earlier relevant studies.
concepts.false: Backward citation searching follows only papers published after the seed article.
concepts.note: It follows cited earlier sources, which must still be checked for eligibility.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Identifying later publications citing a known source.
concepts.example: A citation index finds studies that cite an early therapy trial.
concepts.false: Forward citation searching means reading only an article's own bibliography.
concepts.note: Citation coverage depends on the resource and may be incomplete.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Broad scholarly discovery that can complement structured database searches.
concepts.example: A reviewer uses citation links to locate additional material.
concepts.false: Google Scholar alone guarantees a completely reproducible systematic search.
concepts.note: Record queries and limits while recognizing ranking and coverage limitations.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A record of sources, dates, exact queries, limits and retrieval counts.
concepts.example: The appendix reports each database strategy and search date.
concepts.false: Reporting only the database name makes a search reproducible.
concepts.note: Reproducibility requires enough detail to understand what was actually run.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Adapting concepts to each platform's headings, fields and syntax.
concepts.example: A PubMed strategy is revised before being used in CINAHL.
concepts.false: Copying one database's tags unchanged always works correctly everywhere.
concepts.note: Retain conceptual intent while checking each platform's rules.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The ability to retrieve relevant material rather than miss it.
concepts.example: Additional justified synonyms recover studies omitted by one narrow term.
concepts.false: A search finding very few irrelevant records must have found every relevant study.
concepts.note: Sensitivity and precision are different retrieval goals.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The proportion of retrieved records that are relevant under stated criteria.
concepts.example: More retrieved records meet the review's eligibility criteria after testing refinements.
concepts.false: High precision necessarily proves perfect sensitivity.
concepts.note: A very narrow strategy may appear precise while missing eligible evidence.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Restrictions such as language, date or publication type applied to retrieval.
concepts.example: A date restriction is explicitly justified and reported.
concepts.false: English-only restrictions can never affect a review's evidence base.
concepts.note: Limits can introduce exclusions or bias and should match the question.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Software for organizing bibliographic records, citations and related files.
concepts.example: Zotero stores metadata and generates a selected citation format.
concepts.false: Installing a reference manager guarantees every imported detail is accurate.
concepts.note: Check metadata, duplicates and source identity rather than relying on automation alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A structured comparison table with common information fields across studies.
concepts.example: Rows contain studies and columns summarize design, results and limitations.
concepts.false: An evidence matrix requires copying complete articles into a single cell.
concepts.note: Comparable fields support synthesis across studies rather than file storage alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Restating an idea accurately in original wording while acknowledging its source.
concepts.example: A student changes structure and expression and cites the original study.
concepts.false: Replacing a few words removes the need to cite another author's idea.
concepts.note: Attribution remains necessary even without a direct quotation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Presenting another person's words, ideas or work without appropriate acknowledgment.
concepts.example: A paragraph is copied with no quotation or citation.
concepts.false: A low similarity score proves that all ideas are properly attributed.
concepts.note: Similarity detection and ethical attribution are related but not equivalent checks.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Lec#6  Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An interpretive overview whose scope and selection should be explained.
concepts.example: A thesis background connects theories and findings in a stated area.
concepts.false: Narrative reviewing permits deliberately concealing contrary evidence.
concepts.note: Flexibility does not remove the need for fair, critical and transparent reasoning.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Evidence synthesis using explicit, planned methods to answer a defined question.
concepts.example: Eligibility, searches, screening and appraisal are specified before synthesis.
concepts.false: A systematic review necessarily includes a statistical meta-analysis.
concepts.note: A systematic review can synthesize findings without quantitative pooling.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Systematic mapping of evidence types, concepts and gaps around a broader inquiry.
concepts.example: A review charts what AAC services have been studied and where.
concepts.false: Critical appraisal is forbidden in every scoping review.
concepts.note: Appraisal is not mandatory for all scoping purposes but may be justified.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An advance plan describing how a review will be conducted.
concepts.example: Reviewers prespecify eligibility, sources and synthesis approach.
concepts.false: A protocol can be reconstructed silently after results are known with no consequence.
concepts.note: Prespecification and transparent amendments help distinguish planning from selective decisions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Public recording of review plans in an appropriate registry or repository.
concepts.example: A team checks the scope of a registry before submitting its protocol.
concepts.false: Every review type is eligible for every registry.
concepts.note: Registry coverage and requirements differ; choose a suitable platform.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A reporting guideline for systematic reviews with checklists and flow information.
concepts.example: A report explains identification, screening and included studies.
concepts.false: PRISMA is itself a risk-of-bias assessment instrument.
concepts.note: Reporting completeness and methodological quality require different assessments.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A reporting extension addressing scoping reviews.
concepts.example: A scoping report describes its evidence-charting and selection process.
concepts.false: PRISMA-ScR transforms a mapping review automatically into a treatment-effect meta-analysis.
concepts.note: Use the guideline appropriate to the review's purpose and methods.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A structured scale for assessing aspects of narrative review quality.
concepts.example: A reader examines justification, search description and scientific reasoning.
concepts.false: SANRA is a randomized treatment allocation method.
concepts.note: It concerns narrative review assessment rather than intervention assignment.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Identifying and managing repeated records of the same source.
concepts.example: Database exports containing one article twice are merged appropriately.
concepts.false: Every article with a similar topic is a duplicate and should be removed.
concepts.note: Distinct studies on the same topic must not be mistaken for duplicate records.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Initial eligibility assessment using bibliographic summaries.
concepts.example: Reviewers assess whether a record potentially matches the inclusion criteria.
concepts.false: Abstract screening always makes full-text assessment unnecessary.
concepts.note: Uncertain or potentially eligible records commonly proceed to fuller assessment.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Examination of the report to determine eligibility and extract sufficient information.
concepts.example: A team records why a retrieved paper fails a prespecified criterion.
concepts.false: Full-text exclusions require no stated reason in a transparent review.
concepts.note: Document exclusions so readers can follow selection decisions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Assessment by reviewers separately before resolving differences.
concepts.example: Two reviewers apply criteria and discuss disagreements.
concepts.false: Two names on a paper prove that screening was conducted independently.
concepts.note: Report the actual screening and conflict-resolution procedure.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Transparent reporting of records, reports and studies through selection stages.
concepts.example: Counts distinguish removed duplicates from full-text exclusions.
concepts.false: The number of database records must always equal the number of unique studies.
concepts.note: One study may have multiple reports, and one report may be retrieved repeatedly.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Recording prespecified information from included reports.
concepts.example: Reviewers capture sample, measures, effects and limitations into a form.
concepts.false: Extraction should include only results supporting the reviewer's expectation.
concepts.note: Use consistent fields and verify important information against the source.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Organizing information to map the evidence in a scoping review.
concepts.example: A chart summarizes populations, concepts and service contexts.
concepts.false: Data charting always requires estimating one pooled treatment effect.
concepts.note: Charting can map characteristics without inferential pooling.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Potential systematic deviation of findings from the target truth under a study's methods.
concepts.example: A trial's outcome assessment and missing-data processes are evaluated.
concepts.false: A prestigious journal guarantees low risk of bias in every study.
concepts.note: Judge relevant design features rather than reputation alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A structured tool for assessing risk of bias in randomized trial results.
concepts.example: Reviewers examine domains relevant to an RCT comparison.
concepts.false: RoB 2 is designed only to format Vancouver references.
concepts.note: Match the tool and its version to the study and result being assessed.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A tool family for bias assessment in nonrandomized studies of interventions.
concepts.example: An observational treatment comparison is evaluated for confounding and related bias.
concepts.false: A nonrandomized study needs no assessment of confounding.
concepts.note: Use appropriate guidance; the tool is not a guarantee of causal validity.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Critical appraisal of systematic reviews of randomized or nonrandomized healthcare intervention studies.
concepts.example: A reviewer assesses a review's methods rather than its citation style.
concepts.false: AMSTAR 2 is a replacement name for participant randomization.
concepts.note: Review-level appraisal differs from assessment of individual primary studies.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An appraisal instrument selected for the actual study type and question.
concepts.example: A cohort checklist is chosen for a cohort report.
concepts.false: One generic checklist is perfectly suited to every possible research design.
concepts.note: CASP and JBI offer design-specific resources, not one universal test for everything.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A broad ordering of designs for particular questions, especially intervention effects.
concepts.example: A robust comparative trial may inform an intervention decision.
concepts.false: A high design label overrides serious bias and poor population relevance.
concepts.note: Quality, question fit and applicability modify what a hierarchy alone suggests.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Organizing evidence around related substantive ideas or patterns.
concepts.example: Studies are compared under access, delivery and participation themes.
concepts.false: Synthesis must consist only of one disconnected paragraph per author.
concepts.note: Link findings and limitations across sources to develop an evidence-based account.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Comparing findings in relation to design and measurement differences.
concepts.example: Divergent effects are considered alongside outcome and follow-up differences.
concepts.false: Conflicting findings prove that one author must be dishonest.
concepts.note: Methods, context and uncertainty may explain disagreement without misconduct.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: An argument connecting findings, limitations, contrasts and unresolved questions.
concepts.example: A paragraph identifies agreement, critiques controls and specifies a justified gap.
concepts.false: A synthesis paragraph needs no citations because it discusses several sources.
concepts.note: Attribute the evidence supporting each part of the argument.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A numeric citation convention assigning references in order of first citation.
concepts.example: A source keeps its original number when cited again.
concepts.false: Vancouver requires a new reference number every time the same source reappears.
concepts.note: Reuse the number for the same source and check the required journal variant.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The sequence of sources required by the selected citation system.
concepts.example: A Vancouver list follows citation numbers rather than alphabetical order.
concepts.false: Every reference system requires the same alphabetical ordering.
concepts.note: Citation style determines ordering and punctuation rules.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Checking authors, title, source, date and identifier against the original publication.
concepts.example: A DOI record is checked before a generated citation is retained.
concepts.false: A plausible-looking DOI proves that the cited claim is supported.
concepts.note: Source existence and support for a claim require separate verification.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Importing, checking and organizing bibliographic records before citation.
concepts.example: Records imported by DOI are checked and duplicate entries merged.
concepts.false: Automatic import can never introduce title or author errors.
concepts.note: Clean metadata before relying on generated citations and bibliographies.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Linking in-text citations and bibliography through reference-management software.
concepts.example: A document's reference numbering updates after insertion of a source.
concepts.false: A manually pasted number always remains linked to the bibliography automatically.
concepts.note: Preserve the citation fields and verify the final generated output.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Use of automated support with human verification, privacy protection and accountability.
concepts.example: A researcher checks suggested search terms and verifies each source.
concepts.false: AI-generated citations can be accepted without reading or checking the sources.
concepts.note: Humans remain responsible for accuracy and policy-compliant use.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Generated content that is false, unsupported or misrepresents a source.
concepts.example: A tool supplies a nonexistent article with a plausible title.
concepts.false: A fluent, detailed summary guarantees faithful reporting of the actual study.
concepts.note: Verify existence, methods and findings at the source before relying on the output.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Accountability and transparent reporting of permitted AI assistance under relevant policies.
concepts.example: Authors describe allowed assistance and take responsibility for the work.
concepts.false: An AI system can independently accept research accountability as a human author.
concepts.note: Follow the applicable journal and institutional requirements rather than assume one universal wording.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Avoiding unauthorized disclosure of sensitive research information through tools or services.
concepts.example: Identifiable recordings are not uploaded to unapproved systems.
concepts.false: A convenient tool's popularity proves participant data may be uploaded without authorization.
concepts.note: Consent, security, approvals and data-governance requirements still apply.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Restrictions of discovery tools arising from the sources and links they index.
concepts.example: A mapping tool misses a relevant paper absent from its database.
concepts.false: A visually connected citation map proves a search is complete.
concepts.note: Citation maps support discovery but do not replace systematic search documentation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Question definition, evidence identification, selection, charting and synthesis within a stated approach.
concepts.example: A team charts studies before reporting the pattern of evidence.
concepts.false: A scoping review is defined by omitting an explicit selection process.
concepts.note: Consultation and updated methodological refinements should be justified within the chosen approach.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: Literature Review.pptx; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Coherence between the inquiry, data-generating design and analytical interpretation.
concepts.example: A question about group differences in change uses a justified change-based comparison.
concepts.false: Any available software test answers every pre-post question equivalently.
concepts.note: State the target comparison before selecting a statistical procedure.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A change value calculated as posttest minus pretest under the stated convention.
concepts.example: A score increasing from 12 to 18 has gain 6.
concepts.false: Gain is always pretest divided by posttest.
concepts.note: State score direction because a positive increase is not always clinical improvement.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The average of participants' gain scores within a defined group.
concepts.example: Individual changes are summed and divided by the participant count.
concepts.false: Mean gain necessarily equals the group's posttest mean alone.
concepts.note: With the same complete cases, it equals mean posttest minus mean pretest.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A comparison of average change between groups.
concepts.example: An average gain of 7 versus 3 gives a difference of 4.
concepts.false: Between-group gain difference is calculated by ignoring every baseline observation.
concepts.note: Comparing changes differs from comparing final scores alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A group comparison using final scores rather than individual changes.
concepts.example: Final mean scores are compared without subtracting baseline.
concepts.false: With nonequivalent baseline groups, a final-score difference always isolates treatment effect.
concepts.note: Baseline composition can complicate interpretation of final values.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A comparison of groups formed without random allocation in the relevant study.
concepts.example: Existing therapy appointments determine group membership.
concepts.false: Measuring pretests makes preexisting groups equivalent by definition.
concepts.note: Pretests reveal some differences without eliminating all measured or unmeasured confounding.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Natural development over time as an alternative explanation for observed change.
concepts.example: Children gain language skill during the interval regardless of assigned programme.
concepts.false: Every gain between childhood assessments is necessarily due to therapy.
concepts.note: A suitable comparison can help distinguish intervention-related change from expected development.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Events outside the intervention that influence outcomes during the study.
concepts.example: A new school programme begins while therapy outcomes are measured.
concepts.false: History means only whether the literature review includes old books.
concepts.note: Document concurrent events that might affect the study comparison.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Changes in measurement procedures or instruments affecting observed scores.
concepts.example: A later assessment uses easier prompts than baseline.
concepts.false: Changing the scoring procedure cannot affect apparent treatment gains.
concepts.note: Comparable measurement is necessary to interpret change meaningfully.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Diverging trajectories where baseline-related growth can mimic a treatment difference.
concepts.example: A group starting higher also improves faster before treatment begins.
concepts.false: Any diverging pre-post lines prove a treatment-specific effect.
concepts.note: Additional pretreatment observations can help examine preexisting growth patterns.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The tendency for unusually extreme noisy observations to be less extreme on repeat measurement.
concepts.example: Participants selected for unusually low first scores score closer to average later.
concepts.false: Every movement toward average proves that a treatment caused recovery.
concepts.note: Repeated measures and design evidence help distinguish statistical tendency from genuine change.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Measurement compression near the lower limit of an instrument.
concepts.example: Many participants score zero because the task is too difficult.
concepts.false: A floor effect gives unlimited sensitivity to every further deterioration.
concepts.note: Limited lower range can conceal meaningful differences or changes.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Measurement compression near the upper limit of an instrument.
concepts.example: Participants score near maximum before substantial learning is measured.
concepts.false: A ceiling effect proves that no participant can improve in real life.
concepts.note: A restricted instrument can hide change beyond its measurement range.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Choosing measurement suited to the construct and time scale of expected change.
concepts.example: A targeted probe is evaluated before use over a short therapy interval.
concepts.false: Diagnostic accuracy alone proves sensitivity to all short-term gains.
concepts.note: Assess responsiveness, validity and reliability for the intended purpose.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Assessment against specified task criteria rather than only a normative comparison.
concepts.example: A probe measures accuracy on defined target forms.
concepts.false: A clinician-created probe needs no evidence about scoring or measurement quality.
concepts.note: Target fit is useful but does not replace validation and error assessment.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Consistent measurement meaning and units across repeated observations.
concepts.example: The same interpretable scale is used at pretest and posttest.
concepts.false: Subtracting unrelated instrument scores always yields a meaningful change value.
concepts.note: Confirm measurement comparability before computing or interpreting differences.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Collecting multiple observations before intervention introduction.
concepts.example: Three pretreatment probes show whether performance was already rising.
concepts.false: Two endpoints alone completely reveal every person's growth trajectory.
concepts.note: Additional observations can expose trend and instability hidden by endpoints.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A later observation examining persistence or evolution of outcomes.
concepts.example: A probe after a no-treatment interval evaluates retention.
concepts.false: Follow-up can never add information beyond an immediate posttest.
concepts.note: Specify interval and intervening experiences when interpreting persistence.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Probability of rejecting a false null for a specified alternative under assumptions.
concepts.example: A design is planned for 80% power at a meaningful difference.
concepts.false: Power is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
concepts.note: Power depends on effect, variability, sample size, threshold and design.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Rejecting a true null hypothesis within the specified testing framework.
concepts.example: A test signals a difference when the null is actually true.
concepts.false: Type I error means missing every real effect.
concepts.note: Alpha controls a long-run error property under the stated procedure and assumptions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Failing to reject a false null under a specified alternative.
concepts.example: An underpowered study fails to detect a relevant true effect.
concepts.false: A nonsignificant result establishes that Type II error is impossible.
concepts.note: Beta and power concern behaviour under an alternative, not certainty from one outcome.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A measure of dispersion on the same scale as the observations.
concepts.example: Participants' gain scores vary around their average gain.
concepts.false: Standard deviation is identical to the standard error of the mean.
concepts.note: Spread of individual values differs from uncertainty in an estimated average.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Estimated sampling variability of an estimator under a specified model.
concepts.example: A mean estimate has uncertainty based partly on variability and sample size.
concepts.false: Standard error describes only the range of individual participant scores.
concepts.note: Distinguish estimator uncertainty from the distribution of observations.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A justified comparison of gain values from distinct participant groups.
concepts.example: Two therapy groups' gains are compared under appropriate assumptions.
concepts.false: Gains from different participants always require a paired test merely because each gain uses two scores.
concepts.note: A within-person calculation does not make independent groups paired with each other.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Analysis accounting for linked observations within the same participant or matched pair.
concepts.example: A within-group pre-post difference is analyzed using paired observations.
concepts.false: A paired within-group result by itself establishes superiority over another group.
concepts.note: Within-group change and between-group treatment difference answer different questions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A two-mean comparison that does not impose equal group variances.
concepts.example: Independent gain distributions with unequal variances are compared appropriately.
concepts.false: Every t test requires a pooled equal-variance assumption.
concepts.note: Select the test variant according to design and assumptions.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A model comparing group means for one factor under stated assumptions.
concepts.example: A single factor defines three treatment groups.
concepts.false: A significant omnibus result identifies every pairwise difference without further analysis.
concepts.note: An omnibus comparison and specific contrasts require distinct interpretation.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Modelling follow-up outcomes while accounting for baseline and other justified covariates.
concepts.example: An ANCOVA estimates a conditional group contrast.
concepts.false: Baseline adjustment is forbidden in all nonrandomized studies and automatically unbiased in all randomized studies.
concepts.note: Specify the estimand and assumptions; neither blanket rejection nor automatic causal confidence is justified.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A distinction between an observation distribution and sampling-distribution approximations.
concepts.example: A large sample of skewed observations remains skewed as raw data.
concepts.false: Every raw data set becomes normally distributed once n reaches thirty.
concepts.note: Large-sample approximations have conditions and do not transform the observations.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A difference in means expressed relative to a stated standard deviation convention.
concepts.example: A two-point mean difference divided by SD four equals 0.5.
concepts.false: A standardized effect size itself proves meaningful improvement for every client.
concepts.note: State the denominator convention and examine uncertainty and functional relevance.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A standardized mean-difference estimator with a small-sample bias correction.
concepts.example: A correction factor adjusts an appropriate standardized mean difference.
concepts.false: Hedges g differs from Cohen d solely because it uses any pooled standard deviation.
concepts.note: The small-sample correction is central; denominator choices must also be specified.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: The distinction between participant-level change and a group summary.
concepts.example: The same mean gain can combine diverse individual outcomes.
concepts.false: A positive group mean proves every participant improved equally.
concepts.note: Inspect distributions and individual patterns instead of relying only on averages.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Measurement of meaningful involvement in everyday communication activities.
concepts.example: A caregiver report complements a targeted grammar probe.
concepts.false: Change on an impairment probe automatically captures every everyday participation benefit.
concepts.note: Different outcome domains can complement one another without being interchangeable.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: Examination of how conclusions change under plausible analytical choices or assumptions.
concepts.example: Alternative justified approaches are compared transparently.
concepts.false: Sensitivity analysis means retaining only the model that produces a significant result.
concepts.note: Report prespecified or justified alternatives rather than fishing for favourable findings.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

concepts.definition: A distinction between teaching examples and observations from real participants.
concepts.example: Artificial tutorial scores illustrate a computation without testing real treatment efficacy.
concepts.false: A tutorial's invented teaching dataset proves that its hypothetical treatment works clinically.
concepts.note: The provided PDF explicitly uses a hypothetical scenario and artificial example data.
concepts.referenceSection: Provided handout: PDF Research Question.pdf; relevant methods references below.

sources.title: Chiang, Jhangiani & Price — Research Methods in Psychology, 2nd Canadian edition
sources.use: Accessible reference for research questions, measurement, experiments, surveys, single-case methods and statistical foundations. Original revision explanations are not quotations from the book.

sources.title: Irwin & Donai — Clinical Research Methods in Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology, 4th edition
sources.use: SLP-specific recommended coursebook. Publisher sample and contents checked; full-book access is not claimed.

sources.title: ASHA — Evidence-Based Practice
sources.use: Official guidance on integrating research and individual evidence, expertise and client perspectives.

sources.title: HHS — The Belmont Report
sources.use: Foundational human-research ethics: respect for persons, beneficence and justice. Local institutional review requirements still apply.

sources.title: JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis
sources.use: Methods reference for evidence synthesis, including PCC and scoping reviews. Consult the relevant current chapter.

sources.title: Cooke, Smith & Booth — Beyond PICO: the SPIDER tool for qualitative evidence synthesis
sources.use: Original SPIDER publication record and abstract; complements the provided framework slides.

sources.title: Wildridge & Bell — How CLIP became ECLIPSE
sources.use: Original health-policy/management mnemonic publication. Teaching definitions are grounded in the supplied framework handout.

sources.title: NLM — PubMed User Guide
sources.use: Official reference for Boolean logic, subject headings, field tags and platform-specific search behaviour.

sources.title: PRISMA 2020
sources.use: Official systematic-review reporting guidance; reporting quality is distinct from risk-of-bias assessment.

sources.title: Risk of bias tools — RoB 2
sources.use: Official risk-of-bias resource for randomized trial results; select appropriate tools and versions for other designs.

sources.title: Zotero — Adding Items and metadata
sources.use: Official workflow reference; imported metadata and source interpretations still require verification.

sources.title: NLM — Citing Medicine
sources.use: Reference for biomedical bibliographic formats. Follow the required journal variant for author limits and punctuation.

sources.title: Skoczylas (2019) — Congruence in Research Question, Design, and Analysis
sources.use: The actual tutorial supplied as PDF Research Question.pdf. Its hypothetical scenario and artificial data are teaching material, not an empirical efficacy trial.

sources.title: Cochrane Handbook — Analysis of intervention evidence
sources.use: Methods reference on effects, change scores and baseline adjustment. Analytical choices require attention to the estimand, design and assumptions.
